questions.question: What distinguishes a Parquet encoding from a compression codec?
options: An encoding exploits typed value structure before a codec compresses the resulting bytes
An encoding compresses whole files after a codec rearranges individual typed values
An encoding encrypts column values before a codec stores their schema information
An encoding chooses row groups after a codec computes their minimum and maximum

questions.question: How many bits per dictionary index are needed for a column with 200 distinct values?
options: Seven bits because 200 is below 2 raised to the eighth power
Eight bits because the ceiling of log base 2 of 200 is eight
Sixteen bits because dictionary indexes always use two-byte integers
Two hundred bits because each distinct value needs its own position

questions.question: A million-row status column has four values and is sorted into four long runs. Which combination best exploits its structure?
options: Plain encoding followed by an uncompressed page representation
Delta encoding followed by a high-level Gzip compression pass
Dictionary indexes followed by hybrid run-length and bit-packed encoding
Raw strings followed by a per-row variable-byte integer representation

questions.question: A formerly small Parquet column chunk becomes much larger after values change from country codes to UUIDs. What is the most likely mechanism?
options: Run-length encoding converted every UUID into a repeated country code
Delta encoding replaced UUID values with smaller consecutive time differences
Predicate pushdown duplicated UUID values into every row group footer
The high-cardinality dictionary overflowed its cap and fell back to plain encoding

questions.question: Why can sorting a low-cardinality column improve both pruning and compression?
options: It narrows row-group value ranges and creates long repeated-index runs for RLE
It removes the need for dictionaries and forces every page to use raw strings
It widens row-group value ranges and distributes repeated values across more pages
It converts every column into one globally compressed row-oriented byte stream

questions.question: Which encoding is the best fit for a sorted, steadily increasing timestamp column with mostly small increments?
options: Dictionary encoding of every timestamp as a separate high-cardinality string
Delta binary packing of successive timestamp differences into small integers
Run-length encoding of absolute timestamps that almost never repeat consecutively
Plain encoding with one fixed-width copy of each timestamp in every dictionary

questions.question: Why does decompression speed often matter more than compression speed for analytical data?
options: Analytical files are compressed separately for each query but read only once
Analytical codecs skip compression and perform only repeated dictionary construction
A file is commonly compressed once but decompressed across many subsequent reads
A file is commonly decompressed once but recompressed for every selected column

questions.question: Which codec profile is presented as a strong modern default at low levels?
options: Gzip because it combines the fastest compression with the fastest decompression
Uncompressed because encoded analytical values never contain residual redundancy
LZ4 because it always achieves the highest archival ratio at every compression level
Zstd because it offers a good tunable ratio with fast low-level operation

questions.question: A network-bound scan moves encoded pages over a 200 MB/s path, while Zstd decompression exceeds 800 MB/s. Why can Zstd beat a lighter codec?
options: The CPU work overlaps transfer while the improved ratio reduces the bottleneck bytes
The CPU work disables page encoding while the network receives the original raw bytes
The improved ratio increases transferred bytes while eliminating all decompression work
The slower network forces the query engine to perform random access inside each page

questions.question: The same dataset moves from object storage to local NVMe and queries become CPU-bound on decompression. What adjustment is most defensible?
options: Raise Zstd to its highest level because storage bandwidth is now irrelevant
Use a lighter codec or lower Zstd level to reduce read-path CPU cost
Add dictionary pages to every UUID so the decompressor performs more work
Switch every column to Gzip because its decompression is faster than LZ4

questions.question: Zstd level 19 barely improves the ratio of a sorted dictionary-encoded status column over Snappy. What does this most strongly imply?
options: The page lacks any encoding and therefore needs a second dictionary
The network has already decompressed the values before reading the file
The encoding already removed most redundancy, leaving little for the heavy codec
The row group statistics have expanded the values back to their raw string size

questions.question: Which policy best matches codec choice to data temperature?
options: Use maximum-ratio codecs for every hot table and no compression for archives
Use one codec globally because Parquet cannot vary compression between columns
Use slow legacy compression for hot tables and recompress them for every query
Use fast low-level compression for hot data and stronger Zstd for cold partitions

questions.question: What common principle connects Parquet delta encoding and postings gap encoding?
options: Transform sorted values into small differences, then spend fewer bits on the residuals
Transform sorted values into full strings, then store every value at fixed width
Transform unsorted values into random identifiers, then avoid bit packing entirely
Transform repeated values into row groups, then decode one random value per query

questions.question: Document IDs 1000, 1003, 1007, and 1012 become which gap sequence?
Why does a frequent term often require fewer compressed bits per posting than a rare term?
options: Frequent terms store unsorted document IDs that repeat as long literal strings
Frequent terms omit their document IDs and rely only on collection-level idf
Frequent terms have dense sorted postings whose consecutive document-ID gaps are small
Frequent terms use one Parquet row group while rare terms use an inverted index

questions.question: What access-pattern difference explains why postings formats emphasize fast jumping while Parquet decompresses pages into batches?
options: Postings are written only once, whereas Parquet files are never read after creation
Postings contain typed table leaves, whereas Parquet contains only document identifiers
Postings codecs run offline, whereas Parquet compression sits on every search request
Search scoring traverses and skips within lists, while analytics processes page-sized vectors

questions.question: A timestamp-sorted Parquet table becomes both smaller and easier to prune. Which explanation best unifies the two effects?
options: Sortedness creates small deltas and tight row-group ranges from the same physical order
Sortedness replaces min-max statistics with hashes and expands every timestamp difference
Sortedness makes each timestamp unique and therefore ideal for small dictionary indexes
Sortedness forces page-level random access and disables sequential vectorized decoding

questions.question: Why do both hot search indexes and hot analytical lakes favor fast decoding over maximum compression ratio?
options: Encoding occurs on every read while decoding happens only during initial ingestion
Decoding lies on the repeated read path, so saved bytes must justify added latency and CPU
Maximum-ratio codecs cannot operate on byte streams produced by type-aware encodings
Fast codecs always provide both the smallest files and the lowest CPU usage without tradeoffs
